content: Before traveling, it is essential to review the indications for influenza vaccination and offer the vaccine if deemed appropriate. This is particularly relevant for foreign travelers. Healthcare facility administrators should ensure that influenza vaccines are made available to all personnel before the influenza season begins. This includes staff working in intensive care units (including neonatal ICUs), medical/surgical units, nursing homes, and chronic-care facilities. To improve compliance, strategies such as using mobile carts to deliver vaccines to hospital wards or work sites, and offering vaccines during night and weekend shifts, can be effective. Additionally, follow-up campaigns may be necessary if a community outbreak occurs. Two antiviral agents, amantadine hydrochloride and rimantadine hydrochloride, exhibit specific activity against influenza A viruses. However, only amantadine is licensed for use in the United States. These drugs disrupt the replication cycle of type A influenza viruses, though their exact antiviral mechanisms remain incompletely understood. When administered prophylactically to healthy young adults or children before and during an epidemic, amantadine is approximately 70%-90% effective in preventing illnesses caused by naturally occurring strains of type A influenza viruses. If given within 48 hours of symptom onset to otherwise healthy young adults and children, amantadine can reduce the duration of fever and systemic symptoms, potentially allowing a quicker return to normal activities. It is important to note that while prophylactic antiviral agents may prevent illness, they do not prevent subclinical infections. Consequently, individuals taking these drugs may still develop immune responses that protect them against antigenically related viruses in subsequent years. Side effects of amantadine are rare but may be significant for certain patient groups. In institutional settings housing high-risk individuals, chemoprophylaxis should be initiated promptly during influenza A outbreaks to limit the spread of infection. Contingency plans should be in place to ensure rapid administration of amantadine to residents and staff, including preapproved medication orders or expedited physician orders. All residents of affected institutions should receive amantadine, regardless of prior influenza vaccination status. Dosages should be determined based on the recommendations and precautions outlined in this document and the manufacturer’s package insert. To minimize viral spread and maintain patient care, unvaccinated staff caring for high-risk individuals should also receive chemoprophylaxis. For prophylaxis to be effective, the antiviral drug must be taken daily throughout the period of influenza activity in the community. High-risk individuals vaccinated after the onset of influenza A activity in the community can still benefit from vaccination. However, since antibody development in adults typically takes two weeks post-vaccination, amantadine should be administered during this period. Children receiving the influenza vaccine for the first time may require up to six weeks of prophylaxis, or until two weeks after their second vaccine dose. Amantadine does not interfere with the antibody response to the vaccine. For unvaccinated employees in hospitals, clinics, and chronic-care facilities, chemoprophylaxis should continue for the entire duration of influenza A activity in the community. For those vaccinated during an active influenza A outbreak, chemoprophylaxis should be administered for two weeks post-vaccination. If the outbreak is caused by a variant strain of influenza A not covered by the vaccine, prophylaxis should be considered for all employees, regardless of vaccination status. Chemoprophylaxis may also be indicated for high-risk individuals expected to have a poor antibody response to the influenza vaccine, such as those with advanced HIV infection. However, there is no data on potential interactions between amantadine and other drugs used in managing HIV infection, necessitating close monitoring of these patients if amantadine is administered. For individuals with contraindications to the influenza vaccine, such as anaphylactic hypersensitivity to egg protein or other vaccine components, chemoprophylaxis throughout the influenza season may be appropriate. Amantadine can also be used prophylactically by anyone wishing to avoid influenza A illness, with the decision made on an individual basis between the physician and patient. Amantadine can reduce the severity and duration of influenza A illness in healthy adults. However, there is no evidence to support its efficacy in preventing complications of influenza A in high-risk individuals. As such, no specific recommendations can be made regarding the therapeutic use of amantadine for these patients.
